verses.translation: These are the confidential counsels{H5475} YHWH{H3068} gave{H5414} to Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed One{H4899}, to show{H7200} his servants{H5650} what shall be{H1961} soon{H7138}; and he sent{H7971} them by the hand{H3027} of his messenger{H4397} to his servant{H5650} Yochanan{H3110}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סוֹדוֹת (sodot — 'confidential counsels/secrets', H5475) — the Hebrew wisdom term for the secret deliberation of the divine council (Jer 23:18 — 'Who has stood in the sod of YHWH?'; Ps 25:14 — 'The sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Amos 3:7 — 'He reveals his sod to his servants the prophets'). Greek has Ἀποκάλυψις ('revelation/uncovering'). A back-translator from Greek would use גִּלּוּי (gilui — 'uncovering') or הִתְגַּלּוּת (hitgalut — 'revelation'), never the wisdom-tradition term sod. The Hebrew frames the entire book not as an 'uncovering' but as admission into the divine council's deliberations.

Uses the idiom עַל יַד מַלְאָךְ ('by the hand of a messenger') — a standard Hebrew agency idiom (Ex 9:35, Lev 8:36, Num 15:23, 1 Sam 28:15, 2 Sam 12:25). Greek has ἀποστείλας διὰ τοῦ ἀγγέλου αὐτοῦ ('having sent through his angel'). A back-translator might produce בְּיַד (be-yad) but the full idiom עַל יַד (al yad) is distinctly Hebraic.

Hebrew has שָׁלַח אוֹתָם ('he sent THEM' — plural object) referring to the sodot as multiple discrete counsels. Greek has ἐσήμανεν ('he signified' — treating the content as a singular act). A back-translator from Greek would produce a singular object, not plural. The Hebrew understands the content as multiple confidential counsels, not one unified revelation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'These are the confidential counsels YHWH gave to Yeshua.' Greek: 'The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him.' Different framing — Hebrew uses demonstrative 'these are' and the divine name YHWH; Greek has a titular form and uses θεός ('God').
Hebrew: 'he sent them' (אוֹתָם — plural). Greek: ἐσήμανεν ('he signified'). Different verb and number.
translation_notes: 'Confidential counsels' for sodot preserves the Hebrew concept of admission into a closed divine council. A sod is not merely a 'secret' but a council session and its deliberations.
'By the hand of' for al yad — literal rendering of the Hebrew agency idiom, which implies delegated authority.
textual_notes: Amos 3:7 — 'For the Lord YHWH does nothing unless he has revealed his sod to his servants the prophets.' The Hebrew Revelation opens by identifying itself within this exact prophetic pattern — YHWH's sod delivered to his servants.

verses.translation: Who testified{H5707} the word{H1697} of YHWH{H3068} and the testimony{H5715} from Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed One{H4899}, from all that he saw{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דִּיבּוּר (dibbur — 'speech/utterance') — a specifically Hebrew term for divine speech, used in rabbinic literature for the Ten Commandments (עשרת הדיברות — 'the Ten Speeches/Utterances'). Greek has λόγος ('word/reason') which is far more generic and philosophically loaded. A back-translator from Greek λόγος would use דָּבָר (davar — 'word/thing'), not the specifically divine-speech term dibbur.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the word of YHWH' (הדיבור יהוה). Greek: 'the word of God' (τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ). Hebrew uses the divine name YHWH; Greek uses the generic θεός.
Hebrew: 'from what he saw' (ממה שראה). Greek: 'as many things as he saw' (ὅσα εἶδεν). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: 'Word' for dibbur — though dibbur specifically means 'speech/utterance' (distinct from davar — 'word/thing'), 'word' is used here for readability while noting the Hebrew distinction in the rabbinic tradition.

verses.translation: Holy{H6918} is the one who reads{H7121} and those who hear{H8085} this prophecy{H5016}, and who uphold{H6965} what is written{H3789}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קָדוֹשׁ (kadosh — 'holy', H6918) where Greek has μακάριος ('blessed/happy'). A back-translator from Greek would use אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'blessed is') or מְאֻשָּׁר (me'ushar — 'happy/fortunate'), never kadosh. The Hebrew declares the reader HOLY — set apart for sacred purpose — not merely 'blessed' or 'happy.' This is a fundamentally different theological claim.

Uses וּמְקַיְּימִים (u-meqayyemim — 'who uphold/establish', Piel of קום H6965). Greek has τηροῦντες ('keeping/guarding'). A back-translator would use שׁוֹמְרִים (shomrim — 'keepers/guarders'). The Hebrew meqayyem means to actively ESTABLISH and MAKE STAND what is written — not passively 'keep' or 'observe' it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (kadosh). Greek: 'blessed' (makarios). Fundamentally different attributes — holiness vs. happiness.
Greek adds 'the words of' (τοὺς λόγους) and 'the things written in it' (τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ γεγραμμένα). Hebrew is more concise: 'this prophecy' and 'what is written.'
Greek adds 'for the time is near' (ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς ἐγγύς) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Holy' for kadosh — not 'blessed' — preserving the Hebrew author's theological claim about the reader's status.
'Uphold' for meqayyemim captures the active, establishing sense of the Piel form — these are people who make the word stand.

verses.translation: Yochanan{H3110}, to the seven{H7651} elders{H2205} in Asia: Lovingkindness{H2617} and peace{H7965} be with you, from the one who was{H1961} and is and shall be{H1961}, and from the seven{H7651} spirits{H7307} that are from his throne{H3678}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זְקֵינִים (zekeinim — 'elders', H2205) where Greek has ἐκκλησίαις ('assemblies/churches'). No back-translator from Greek would render ἐκκλησία as 'elder.' The Hebrew views the seven communities through their leadership — the letter goes to the ELDERS, not to abstract assemblies. This is consistent with Jewish communal structure where the zekeinim govern the congregation.

Uses חֶסֶד (chesed — 'lovingkindness/covenant loyalty', H2617) where Greek has χάρις ('grace'). A back-translator would use חֵן (chen — 'grace/favor'), not the theologically loaded covenant term chesed. Chesed is YHWH's covenant faithfulness (Ex 34:6-7 — 'abounding in chesed and truth'; the refrain of Psalm 136), fundamentally different from the Greek concept of charis.

Hebrew parses the divine name through three tenses of היה: שֶׁהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('who was and is and shall be'). All three forms derive from the root היה — the same root as the name YHWH. Greek has ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('the one who is, who was, and the coming one') — switching to ἔρχομαι ('to come') for the future, breaking the root pattern. The Hebrew maintains the etymological connection to the divine name throughout; a back-translator from Greek would break it.

Hebrew: spirits 'from his throne' (מִכִּסְאוֹ — min, 'from/out of'). Greek: spirits 'before his throne' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου — 'in front of'). 'From' implies emanation/origin; 'before' implies position. A back-translator from Greek would use לִפְנֵי (lifnei — 'before'), not מִן (min — 'from').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'elders' (zekeinim). Greek: 'assemblies/churches' (ekklesiai). Entirely different addressees.
Hebrew: 'lovingkindness' (chesed). Greek: 'grace' (charis). Different theological concept.
Hebrew: 'shall be' (yihyeh — future of היה). Greek: 'the coming one' (erchomenos — from erchomai, 'to come'). Different verb entirely for the future aspect.
Hebrew: 'from his throne' (mi-kis'o). Greek: 'before his throne' (enopion tou thronou). Different preposition with different theology — emanation vs. position.
translation_notes: 'Lovingkindness' for chesed — preserving the covenant-loyalty dimension that 'grace' lacks.
'Elders' for zekeinim — the Hebrew word specifically denotes community leaders, not congregations.
textual_notes: Exodus 34:6 — 'YHWH, YHWH, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in chesed and truth.' Chesed is YHWH's defining covenantal attribute.

Exodus 3:14 — 'I will be what I will be' (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה). The three-tense parsing of YHWH in this verse (was/is/shall be) reflects the Hebrew understanding of the divine name as containing all tenses of the verb 'to be.'

verses.translation: And from Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed One{H4899}, the faithful{H539} witness{H5707}, and first{H7223} who rose{H6965} from the dead{H4191}, and ruler{H5057} and commander{H6680} over the earth{H776} — who loved{H157} us and washed{H7364} us from our iniquities{H5771} with his blood{H1818}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נָגִיד וּמְצַוֶּה (nagid u-metsavveh — 'ruler and commander') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 55:4: הֵן עֵד לְאוּמִּים נְתַתִּיו נָגִיד וּמְצַוֵּה לְאֻמִּים ('Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a ruler and commander to the peoples'). The Hebrew combines 'faithful witness' and 'ruler and commander' from a single Isaiah verse. Greek has ὁ ἄρχων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς ('the ruler of the kings of the earth') — departing entirely from Isaiah 55:4. A back-translator from Greek would never produce the Isaiah quote.

Uses רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁקָּם מֵהַמֵּתִים ('first who ROSE from the dead') with the active verb קָם (qam — 'rose/stood up', H6965). Greek has πρωτότοκος τῶν νεκρῶν ('firstborn of the dead'). A back-translator would use בְּכוֹר (bechor — 'firstborn'), not rishon she-qam. The Hebrew emphasizes the ACT of rising; the Greek emphasizes the STATUS of being firstborn.

Uses מֵעֲווֹנותֵינוּ (me-avonotenu — 'from our iniquities', H5771). Greek has ἐκ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ('from sins'). A back-translator would use חַטָּאת (chatat — 'sin') to match ἁμαρτία, not עָוֹן (avon — 'iniquity/twisted deed'). The Hebrew specifies the nature of the offense as crookedness/perversion — the עוון of Isaiah 53:5-6.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'first who rose from the dead.' Greek: 'firstborn of the dead.' Different concept — active resurrection vs. birth-order status.
Hebrew: 'ruler and commander over the earth' (Isaiah 55:4 verbatim). Greek: 'ruler of the kings of the earth.' Different scope.
Hebrew: 'washed us' (rachatztenu — from rachats, H7364). Some Greek MSS: λύσαντι ('freed/loosed us'); others: λούσαντι ('washed us'). Hebrew unambiguously reads 'washed.'
Hebrew: 'from our iniquities' (avonotenu). Greek: 'from our sins' (hamartion). Different Hebrew sin-concept.
translation_notes: 'Ruler and commander' for nagid u-metsavveh — preserving the Isaiah 55:4 allusion. Nagid (H5057) is the title for Israel's appointed leaders (1 Sam 9:16, 2 Sam 5:2). Metsavveh (from tsavah, H6680) means 'one who commands/orders.'
'Washed' for rachats (H7364) — the verb for ritual washing/bathing (Gen 18:4, Ex 2:5, Lev 15:5-13). Connects cleansing from iniquity to Levitical purification.
textual_notes: Isaiah 55:4 — the source for both 'witness' (ed) and 'ruler and commander' (nagid u-metsavveh) applied to the messianic figure in a single verse.

verses.translation: And he made{H6213} us into kings{H4428} and priests{H3548} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068} and his father{H1}. To him shall be glory{H3519} and splendor{H8597} from eternity{H5769} and unto eternity{H5769}. Amen{H543}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כָּבוֹד וְתִפְאֶרֶת ('glory and splendor') where Greek has δόξα καὶ κράτος ('glory and might/dominion'). A back-translator from Greek would use כָּבוֹד וּגְבוּרָה (kavod u-gevurah — 'glory and might') or כָּבוֹד וָעֹז (kavod va-oz — 'glory and strength'), not tiferet. The Hebrew pair kavod ve-tiferet echoes priestly language — Exodus 28:2: לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת ('for glory and for splendor,' describing the priestly garments).

Uses לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה ('before YHWH') where Greek has τῷ θεῷ ('to/for God'). Hebrew uses the divine name and the spatial preposition 'before/in the presence of'; Greek uses a generic title and a dative of advantage. A back-translator from Greek would write לֵאלֹהִים (le-Elohim — 'to/for God'), not lifnei YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'glory and splendor' (kavod ve-tiferet). Greek: 'glory and might' (doxa kai kratos). Different attribute paired with glory.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH and his father.' Greek: 'to God and his Father.' Different divine name and different preposition.
Hebrew: 'from eternity and unto eternity' (me-olam ve-ad olam). Greek: 'unto the ages of the ages' (eis tous aionas ton aionon). Different temporal formula — Hebrew bilateral; Greek directional.
translation_notes: The pair 'glory and splendor' (kavod ve-tiferet) directly echoes Exodus 28:2, connecting the believers' priestly status to the Aaronic priesthood's garments.
'Kings' for melachim — the Hebrew is unambiguously plural 'kings,' not the ambiguous Greek βασιλείαν (which some MSS read as 'kingdom,' singular).
textual_notes: Exodus 19:6 — 'And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests (mamlechet kohanim) and a holy nation.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes this Sinai promise.
Exodus 28:2 — 'And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for splendor (le-khavod u-le-tifaret).' The same word pair applied to the new priesthood.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! He shall come{H935} in a cloud{H6051}, and those who pierced{H1856} him shall see{H7200} him, and all{H3605} the families{H4940} of the earth{H776} shall weep{H1058}. Yes{H3651}, amen{H543}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת (ha-mishpachot — 'the families/clans', H4940) where Greek has φυλαί (phulai — 'tribes'). A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁבָטִים (shevatim — 'tribes'), NOT mishpachot. The Hebrew echoes Zechariah 12:12-14 which uses מִשְׁפְּחוֹת repeatedly: 'the land shall mourn, every family (mishpachah) by itself' — listing the families of David, Nathan, Levi, and Shimei. The Hebrew preserves Zechariah's exact vocabulary.

Uses הַדֹּקְרִים (ha-doqerim — 'those who pierced', H1856) — the EXACT root from Zechariah 12:10: וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר דָּקָרוּ ('and they shall look upon me whom they pierced'). The verb דקר is rare in the OT (Num 25:8, Judg 9:54, 1 Sam 31:4, Zech 12:10). The Hebrew Revelation applies the Zechariah prophecy with its own verb.

Uses singular בֶּעָנָן ('in a cloud') where Greek has plural μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν ('with the clouds'). The singular cloud evokes the Shekinah — the pillar of cloud (Ex 13:21-22), the cloud over the Tabernacle (Ex 40:34-38), the cloud on Sinai (Ex 24:15-18). A back-translator from Greek plural would write בֶּעָנָנִים (be-ananim).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in a cloud' (singular — Shekinah imagery). Greek: 'with the clouds' (plural).
Hebrew lacks 'every eye shall see him' (πᾶς ὀφθαλμός ὄψεται αὐτόν). The Hebrew restricts the seeing to 'those who pierced him.'
Hebrew: 'shall weep' (yivku — from bakah, H1058 — 'to cry/weep'). Greek: κόψονται ('shall beat themselves in mourning'). Different mourning action — tears vs. self-striking.
translation_notes: 'Families' for mishpachot, not 'tribes' — preserving the Zechariah 12:12 allusion where mourning is organized by families.
'In a cloud' (singular) to preserve the Shekinah connection.
textual_notes: Zechariah 12:10 — 'And they shall look upon me whom they pierced (דקרו), and they shall mourn for him.' The Hebrew combines Daniel 7:13 (cloud coming) with Zechariah 12:10 (piercing/mourning) using Zechariah's own vocabulary.
Daniel 7:13 (Aramaic) — 'with the clouds of heaven (עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא) one like a son of man came.' The Hebrew singular ענן vs. Daniel's Aramaic plural ענני is a deliberate choice.

verses.translation: I am the first{H7223} and the last{H314}, the beginning and the end{H5490}, says{H559} the Lord{H113}, the Mighty One{H117} — who was{H1961} and is and shall be{H1961}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. Greek has τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω ('the Alpha and the Omega'). If the Hebrew were back-translated from Greek, the translator would write הָאָלֶף וְהַתָּו ('the Aleph and the Tav') — using Hebrew letters. Instead, the Hebrew preserves Isaiah's self-declaration of YHWH. The Greek translator converted the Hebrew prophetic concept to Greek letter-symbolism. This is among the strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation.

Uses הָאָדוֹן אַדִּיר ('the Lord, the Mighty One') — two Hebrew titles. אָדוֹן (Adon, H113 — 'Lord/Master') and אַדִּיר (addir, H117 — 'mighty/majestic', Ps 8:1, 93:4, Isa 33:21). Greek has κύριος ὁ θεός... ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God... the Almighty'). A back-translator would use אֵל שַׁדַּי (El Shaddai) or שַׁדַּי for παντοκράτωρ, not the poetic addir.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the first and the last' (Isaiah 44:6 quote). Greek: 'the Alpha and the Omega' (Greek letter metaphor). Entirely different expressions.
Hebrew includes 'the beginning and the end' (techilat ve-ha-sof). This phrase is NOT in the standard Greek of v8 — some MSS add ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, likely harmonized from 21:6.
Hebrew: 'the Lord, the Mighty One' (ha-Adon addir). Greek: 'the Lord God... the Almighty' (Kurios ho Theos... ho Pantokrator). Different divine titles.
translation_notes: 'Mighty One' for addir (H117) — a poetic Hebrew title. In Psalm 93:4, YHWH is called אַדִּיר בַּמָּרוֹם ('mighty on high').
'Beginning' for techilat — a later Hebrew form without a standard Strong's number, from the root חלל.
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — 'Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, YHWH of hosts: I am the first and I am the last (אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן); besides me there is no god.'
Isaiah 48:12 — 'I am he; I am the first, I also am the last (אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן אַף אֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן).'

verses.translation: I, Yochanan{H3110}, was{H1961} on the island{H339} called{H7121} Patmos, on account of the word{H1697} of YHWH{H3068} and the testimony{H5715} from Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed One{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אִי (i — 'island', H339) — the standard OT word for islands/coastlands (Gen 10:5, Isa 11:11, 42:4, 42:10, 49:1, 51:5, 60:9, Jer 31:10). The Hebrew author naturally uses the biblical term embedded in distinctly Hebrew syntax: בָּאִי הַנִּקְרָא ('on the island called').

Completely OMITS the Greek self-identification: 'your brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Yeshua the Anointed' (ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὑμῶν καὶ συγκοινωνός...). The Hebrew has a far more concise introduction. If the Hebrew were back-translated from Greek, this entire phrase would be included.
greek_deviations: Hebrew omits 'your brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Yeshua the Anointed' — entirely present in Greek.
Hebrew: 'the word of YHWH.' Greek: 'the word of God.' Again, YHWH vs. θεός.
translation_notes: 'On account of' for bishvil — a distinctly post-biblical Hebrew preposition not found in the OT. Its presence confirms the text's composition in a living, later register of Hebrew, not mechanical back-translation from Greek.

verses.translation: And the Holy{H6944} Spirit{H7307} rested upon me, and I heard{H8085} from behind{H310} me a great{H1419} voice{H6963}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שׁוֹרֶה עָלַי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ ('the Holy Spirit rested upon me') — using the verb שורה (to rest/dwell), semantically equivalent to שכן (shakan) — the root of שְׁכִינָה (Shekinah). The standard rabbinic expression for prophetic inspiration is רוח הקודש שורה עליו ('the Holy Spirit rests upon him'). Greek ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι ('I became/was in the Spirit') is entirely different — a state of being, not a divine presence descending upon someone. A back-translator from Greek would write הָיִיתִי בָּרוּחַ ('I was in the spirit'), never שׁוֹרֶה עָלַי ('it rested upon me').
Hebrew OMITS 'on the Lord's day' (ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ). This significant Greek phrase — a cornerstone of Christian Sunday theology — is completely absent from the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy Spirit rested upon me' (Shekinah language). Greek: 'I was in the Spirit' (state description). Fundamentally different prophetic mode.
Hebrew omits 'on the Lord's day' entirely.
Greek adds 'like a trumpet' (ὡς σάλπιγγος) to describe the voice — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Rested upon me' for shorah alai — preserving the Shekinah theology. The Spirit is not something Yochanan enters into; it descends upon him as upon the prophets of old.
שׁוֹרֶה (shorah) lacks a standard Strong's number — it is a post-biblical Hebrew verb meaning 'to rest/dwell upon,' related to the concept of Shekinah.
textual_notes: Numbers 11:25 — 'And YHWH came down in the cloud and took of the spirit that was upon him and placed it upon the seventy elders. And when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied.' The same pattern of the spirit 'resting upon' for prophetic inspiration.
Isaiah 11:2 — 'And the spirit of YHWH shall rest upon him (וְנָחָה עָלָיו רוּחַ יהוה).' The Shekinah resting pattern for messianic/prophetic inspiration.

verses.translation: And it said{H559}: I am the first{H7223} and the last{H314}. And all{H3605} that you saw{H7200}, write{H3789} in the scroll{H5612} and send{H7971} it to the elders{H2205} in Asia: to Ephesus and also{H1571} to Smyrna, and to Pergamum and also{H1571} to Thyatira, and to Sardis and also{H1571} to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') where Greek has Ἄλφα καὶ Ὦ ('Alpha and Omega'). Same one-way marker as v8 — Isaiah quote vs. Greek letter metaphor.
Again uses זְקֵינִים (zekeinim — 'elders') where Greek has ἐκκλησίαι ('assemblies/churches'). Same one-way marker as v4.

Uses feminine verb וְאָמְרָה (ve-amrah — 'and she said') for the voice. Hebrew קוֹל (qol — 'voice') takes feminine agreement in Hebrew (Jer 10:13, Job 30:31). This is a natural Hebrew grammatical feature — a back-translator might reproduce it, but only if natively thinking in Hebrew gender agreement.

Hebrew groups the cities with וְגַם ('and also'): Ephesus-and-also-Smyrna, Pergamum-and-also-Thyatira, Sardis-and-also-Philadelphia-and-Laodicea. Greek simply lists them sequentially with καὶ εἰς ('and to'). The Hebrew grouping suggests a deliberate pairing of communities. A back-translator from Greek's flat list would not invent this grouping.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the first and the last.' Greek: 'the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last.' Greek has BOTH titles; Hebrew has only the Isaiah quotation.
Hebrew: 'to the elders in Asia.' Greek: 'to the seven assemblies in Asia.' Different addressees.
Hebrew: 'what you saw' (she-ra'ita — past tense). Greek: 'what you see' (ho blepeis — present tense).
translation_notes: City names are transliterated into Hebrew phonology: עפהיזום, סמירנין, פירגימום, טיאטירס, זארדיס, פילדלפיאן, לאדיצאן. These are foreign place names adapted to Hebrew speech, suggesting oral transmission through Hebrew-speaking channels.

verses.translation: And I turned{H2015} to see{H7200} the voice{H6963} that was speaking{H1696} with me, and when I turned{H2015} I saw{H7200} seven{H7651} menorot{H4501} of gold{H2091}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָפַכְתִּי (hafachti — 'I turned', from הפך H2015 — 'to turn/overturn') — the word for God overturning Sodom (Gen 19:21,25,29), turning water to blood (Ex 7:17), turning mourning to dancing (Ps 30:11), turning a curse to blessing (Deut 23:5). Greek ἐπέστρεψα (epestrepsa) means simply 'I turned around.' A back-translator from Greek would use פָּנִיתִי (paniti — 'I turned/faced') or שַׁבְתִּי (shavti — 'I returned'), not the theologically loaded hafach.

Uses מְנוֹרוֹת (menorot — 'lampstands/menorot', H4501) — the specific Temple word from Exodus 25:31-40 for the golden Menorah of the Tabernacle and Temple. Greek λυχνίας (luchnias) is generic 'lampstands.' The Hebrew author naturally draws on Temple vocabulary — the seven lampstands are seven menorot.
translation_notes: 'Menorot' is preserved untranslated — these are the specific Temple lampstands, Israel's iconic seven-branched symbol.
שֶׁל (shel — 'of') is a post-biblical Hebrew particle, replacing the biblical construct chain. Its presence confirms the text was composed in spoken/later Hebrew.
textual_notes: Zechariah 4:2 — 'And he said to me, What do you see? And I said, I see a menorah (מנורה) all of gold.' The prophetic menorah vision connects directly to Zechariah.
Exodus 25:31-37 — YHWH's instructions for the golden menorah in the Tabernacle. The menorot vision echoes the original divine design.

verses.translation: And between{H996} them, one{H259} like the likeness{H1823} of a man{H120}, and clothed{H3847} in tunics{H3801} of white{H3836}, and girded{H2296} upon the breast{H2373} with a girdle{H2290} of gold{H2091}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כִּדְמוּת אָדָם ('like the likeness of a man') — NOT 'like a son of man' (כבן אדם/כבר אנש). The word דְּמוּת (demut, H1823 — 'likeness/image') appears in Genesis 1:26 (כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'according to our likeness') and crucially in Ezekiel 1:26 (כִּדְמוּת אָדָם — 'like the likeness of a man' — describing the figure on the divine throne). Greek has ὅμοιον υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου ('like a son of man'). A back-translator from Greek would write כְּבֶן אָדָם (ke-ven adam — 'like a son of man'), NOT ki-demut adam. The Hebrew connects the vision to BOTH Genesis creation (man in God's image) AND Ezekiel's throne vision.

Uses כֻתּוֹנוֹת (kutonot — 'tunics/coats', H3801, PLURAL) — the word for: (a) the coats of skin God made for Adam and Eve (Gen 3:21), (b) Joseph's coat (Gen 37:3), (c) the priestly inner garment (Ex 28:4,39-40). Greek has ποδήρη ('foot-length garment') — a descriptive term about length, not a loaded Hebrew word. A back-translator from Greek would describe the garment's length, not use the priestly/Genesis vocabulary. The plural 'tunics' is also unusual for one person — possibly indicating layered priestly garments.

Uses חָזֶה (chazeh — 'breast', H2373) — in OT usage, this is primarily the breast of the sacrificial peace offering waved before YHWH (Ex 29:26-27, Lev 7:30-31, 8:29, 10:14-15). The Hebrew author describes the figure's chest with sacrificial vocabulary. Greek μαστοῖς is anatomically neutral.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like the likeness of a man' (ki-demut adam — Ezekiel 1:26 language). Greek: 'like a son of man' (Daniel/Gospel language). Different OT source text.
Hebrew: 'tunics of white' (kutonot lavan — priestly garments + white). Greek: 'a garment reaching to the feet' (podere — description of length). Different description entirely.
Hebrew specifies 'white' (lavan) for the garments — Greek does not mention color for the main robe.
translation_notes: 'Likeness of a man' for ki-demut adam — preserving the Genesis 1:26/Ezekiel 1:26 connection. This is NOT 'son of man' — it is an earlier, more creation-rooted expression.
'Tunics' for kutonot — the priestly inner garments from Exodus 28:4.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:26 — 'And above the firmament was the likeness of a throne, and upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness like the appearance of a man (כִּדְמוּת אָדָם) upon it above.' The Hebrew Revelation places the same demut adam figure among the menorot.
Genesis 1:26 — 'Let us make man in our image (בְּצַלְמֵנוּ), according to our likeness (כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ).' The demut vocabulary binds the heavenly figure to the creation narrative.

verses.translation: But his head{H7218} and his hair{H8181} were white{H3836} like wool{H6785}, white{H3836}; and his eyes{H5869} like a flame{H3851} of fire{H784}.

one_way_hebrew: The emphatic double לָבָן ('white... white') is a Hebrew intensification technique — repeating an adjective for emphasis (cf. 'holy, holy, holy' in Isa 6:3; 'comfort, comfort' in Isa 40:1). Greek adds a DIFFERENT simile — 'like snow' (ὡς χιών) — rather than intensifying the wool comparison. A back-translator from Greek 'white as wool, white as snow' would include both similes, not produce the Hebrew doubling pattern.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'like snow' (ὡς χιών) after 'like white wool.' Hebrew has only 'white like wool, white' — using emphatic repetition instead of a second simile.
translation_notes: 'White like wool, white' — preserving the Hebrew emphatic doubling.
אֲבָל (aval — 'but/however') is a post-biblical Hebrew conjunction, not found with this meaning in the OT. Another marker of the text's later Hebrew register.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:9 — 'His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like pure wool (כַּעֲמַר נְקֵא).' Both Daniel and the Hebrew Revelation connect white wool to the divine figure, but Daniel uses the Aramaic עמר (amar) while the Hebrew uses צֶמֶר (tsemer — the Hebrew word for wool).

verses.translation: And his feet{H7272} like bronze{H5178}, and his voice{H6963} like a roar{H7494} of great{H1419} waters{H4325}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כְּרַעַשׁ מַיִם גְּדוֹלִים ('like a roar of great waters') with רַעַשׁ (ra'ash — 'earthquake/roar/tumult', H7494). Greek has φωνὴ ὑδάτων πολλῶν ('sound of many waters'). Hebrew ra'ash is far more violent than Greek phone — it is the word for earthquakes (1 Kings 19:11-12), theophanic trembling (Ezek 3:12-13), and cosmic upheaval (Isa 29:6). A back-translator from Greek 'sound/voice' would use קוֹל (qol — 'voice/sound'), not ra'ash.

Uses כִּנְחוֹשֶׁת (ki-nechoshet — 'like bronze', H5178) — the simple, standard OT word for copper/bronze. Greek has χαλκολιβάνῳ (chalkolibanon — a mysterious compound, perhaps 'fine brass/bronze') that scholars still debate. The Hebrew uses the plain, well-known biblical word; the Greek has a rare compound unique to Revelation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like bronze' (nechoshet — standard, clear). Greek: 'like chalkolibanon' (obscure compound).
Greek adds 'as if refined in a furnace' (ὡς ἐν καμίνῳ πεπυρωμένοι) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'roar' (ra'ash) of waters. Greek: 'sound/voice' (phone) of waters. Different intensity — seismic vs. auditory.
translation_notes: 'Roar' for ra'ash captures the seismic, terrifying quality absent from the Greek 'sound.'
'Bronze' for nechoshet (H5178) — the standard OT word, used for the bronze serpent (Num 21:9), Temple vessels (1 Kings 7:14), and Ezekiel's bronze-like figure (Ezek 40:3).
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:24 — 'I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of great waters (כְּקוֹל מַיִם רַבִּים), like the voice of the Almighty.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes Ezekiel but intensifies 'sound' (qol) to 'roar' (ra'ash).
Ezekiel 43:2 — 'The glory of the God of Israel came from the east, and his voice was like the sound of many waters (כְּקוֹל מַיִם רַבִּים).' The theophanic voice-as-waters motif is deeply Ezekielian.

verses.translation: And seven{H7651} stars{H3556} in his right{H3225} hand{H3027}, and from his mouth{H6310} goes forth{H1980} a double-edged{H6374} sword{H2719}, and his appearance{H4758} shining{H2224} like the sun{H8121}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת ('sword of double-edges/mouths') coming from מִפִּיו ('his mouth'). The word פִּיפִיּוֹת (pifiyyot, H6374) comes from פֶּה (peh — 'mouth'), literally meaning 'mouths.' A sword of 'mouths' comes from his 'mouth' — this is a naturally occurring Hebrew wordplay between פִּיו (piv — 'his mouth') and פִּיפִיּוֹת (pifiyyot — 'mouths/edges'). Greek ῥομφαία δίστομος ὀξεῖα ('sharp two-mouthed sword') from στόματος ('mouth') does preserve the mouth/edge connection, but the Hebrew pun is tighter — the SAME root פ-ה appears in both words organically. Psalm 149:6 uses the identical phrase חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת.

Uses זֹרֵחַ (zore'ach — 'shining/rising', H2224) — the specific word for the sun rising/dawning (Judg 9:33, 2 Sam 23:4, 2 Kings 3:22, Ps 104:22, Isa 60:1, Mal 3:20). Greek φαίνει ('shines') is generic. The Hebrew implies the figure's appearance is like the sun AT ITS RISING — the moment of maximum dramatic effect.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὀξεῖα ('sharp') to describe the sword — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds ἐν τῇ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ ('in his power/strength') to describe the sun — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Double-edged' for pifiyyot — literally 'of mouths.' The peh/pifiyyot wordplay with the sword coming from his mouth is a Hebrew literary feature.
'Shining' for zore'ach — the sunrise verb, implying dawn-like brilliance.
textual_notes: Psalm 149:6 — 'Let the high praises of God be in their throat, and a two-edged sword (חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת) in their hand.' The same phrase connects praise from the mouth with a sword of mouths.
Malachi 3:20 (4:2 in English) — 'But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise (וְזָרְחָה) with healing in its wings.' Same root zarach in a messianic context.

verses.translation: And when I saw{H7200} him, I fell{H5307} at his feet{H7272} like a dead man{H4191}. And he laid{H5117} his right{H3225} hand{H3027} upon me and said{H559} to me: Do not fear{H3372}. I am the first{H7223} and the last{H314}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַנִּיחַ (maniach — 'laid/placed', from נוח H5117 — 'to rest'). This is the root of Noah's name (Gen 5:29) and carries connotations of rest, comfort, and sabbath peace. Greek ἔθηκε (etheke — 'placed/set') is neutral. The Hebrew says the figure 'rested' his hand upon Yochanan — an act of comfort using the 'rest' vocabulary. The same root appears in Genesis 2:15 where God 'placed/rested' (vayyanach) Adam in the garden.
translation_notes: 'Laid' for maniach — from the root nuach (rest). The comfort dimension of nuach is part of the meaning: the divine hand brings rest to the terrified prophet.
textual_notes: Isaiah 41:10,13 — 'Fear not, for I am with you... I, YHWH your God, hold your right hand.' The 'do not fear' combined with the right hand echoes Isaiah's encouragement.
Daniel 10:9-10 — Daniel also fell as if dead before a heavenly vision and was touched and raised. The Hebrew Revelation follows the same prophetic encounter pattern.

verses.translation: And see{H7200}: I was{H1961} dead{H4191}, and now I am alive{H2416} from eternity{H5769} and unto eternity{H5769}. And I have the keys{H4668} of death{H4194} and of Geihinnom{H1516}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַגֵּיהִנֹּם (ha-Geihinnom — 'Gei Hinnom / Valley of Hinnom') where Greek has ᾅδου (Hadou — 'Hades'). Geihinnom is the HEBREW geographical name for the valley south of Jerusalem (Josh 15:8, 18:16, 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chr 28:3, 33:6, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2, 32:35) where child sacrifices were performed and which became the symbol of divine judgment. A back-translator from Greek Hades would use שְׁאוֹל (Sheol — the Hebrew underworld), NOT Geihinnom. The use of the specific Palestinian geographical name — a place you could walk to from the Temple Mount — is a powerful indicator of Hebrew origin.

Uses וְעַכְשָׁיו (ve-achshav — 'and now') — a colloquial Hebrew adverb typical of spoken/post-biblical Hebrew. This is NOT the biblical עַתָּה (attah — 'now') but the later form עכשיו. Its presence confirms the text was composed in a living Hebrew register, not mechanically back-translated from Greek.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from eternity and unto eternity') — a standard Hebrew liturgical formula (Ps 41:13, 90:2, 103:17, 106:48). Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). The Hebrew bilateral 'from-to' formula is different from the Greek directional 'unto.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Geihinnom' (Valley of Hinnom — Palestinian geography). Greek: 'Hades' (Greek underworld). Entirely different conceptual frameworks.
Greek adds ἀμήν ('amen') — absent from Hebrew here.
Hebrew: 'and now' (ve-achshav). Greek: 'and behold' (kai idou). Different interjection.
translation_notes: 'Geihinnom' preserved untranslated — this is the specific Hebrew geographical/theological term. Translating as 'hell' imports later theology.
'From eternity and unto eternity' for me-olam ve-ad olam — the Psalmic liturgical formula.
עַכְשָׁיו (achshav) lacks a standard Strong's number — it is a post-biblical Hebrew adverb.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 7:31-32 — 'And they built the high places of Tophet in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (בְּגֵי בֶן הִנֹּם) to burn their sons and daughters in fire... it shall no more be called Tophet or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.' Geihinnom's association with judgment derives from this prophetic condemnation.

verses.translation: Write{H3789} what you saw{H7200} and what shall be{H1961} after{H310} this.

greek_deviations: Hebrew has TWO temporal categories: 'what you saw' (past) and 'what shall be after this' (future). Greek has THREE: 'what you saw' (past, ἃ εἶδες), 'what is/are' (present, ἃ εἰσίν), and 'what is about to happen after these things' (future, ἃ μέλλει γενέσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα). The Hebrew omits the present-tense category entirely.
translation_notes: 'After this' for achar kach — a standard Hebrew temporal phrase.

verses.translation: And the secret counsel{H5475} of the seven{H7651} stars{H3556} that you saw{H7200} in my right{H3225} hand{H3027}, and the seven{H7651} menorot{H4501} of gold{H2091}: thus it is — the seven{H7651} stars{H3556}, these are seven{H7651} messengers{H4397}, and the seven{H7651} menorot{H4501} are seven{H7651} elders{H2205}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סוֹד (sod — 'secret counsel', H5475) again — as in v1. Greek has μυστήριον ('mystery'). A back-translator from Greek μυστήριον would use רָז (raz — the Aramaic/Daniel word for 'mystery', Dan 2:18-19,27-30,47) or the later Hebrew form, not the Hebrew wisdom-tradition term sod. The sod is the divine council's deliberation (Ps 25:14 — 'The sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Prov 3:32 — 'his sod is with the upright'; Jer 23:18 — 'who has stood in the sod of YHWH?').

CRITICAL: Uses זְקֵינִים (zekeinim — 'elders', H2205) where Greek has ἐκκλησίαι ('assemblies/churches'). The seven menorot ARE the seven ELDERS — not 'churches.' The Hebrew identifies the lampstands with the LEADERS of the communities, while Greek identifies them with the communities themselves. This is a fundamentally different ecclesiology — leadership-centered vs. congregation-centered — that a back-translator from Greek would never produce. In Jewish communal structure, the elders ARE the community's embodiment.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the seven menorot are seven elders.' Greek: 'the seven lampstands are seven assemblies/churches.' Different identification of the lampstands — leaders vs. congregations.
Hebrew: 'the secret counsel' (sod). Greek: 'the mystery' (musterion). Different concept — sod implies a deliberative council's proceedings; musterion implies hidden knowledge.
translation_notes: 'Secret counsel' for sod — not 'mystery.' The sod is the divine council's deliberation (see v1 notes).
'Elders' for zekeinim — the menorot represent not abstract assemblies but their governing leaders.
textual_notes: The identification of menorot with elders/leaders echoes Zechariah 4, where the menorah is connected to Zerubbabel (the leader) and the 'two anointed ones.' The menorah represents light-bearing leadership.

The shift from zekeinim (v4, v11, v20) to ekklesia in the Greek is systematic — every instance where the Hebrew has 'elders,' the Greek has 'churches.' This suggests a deliberate Greek editorial decision, not a translation variant.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 1 in Hebrew presents itself not as an 'apocalypse' (Greek apokalupsis — uncovering) but as confidential divine counsels (Hebrew sodot) delivered through prophetic channels. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers where the Hebrew could not derive from the Greek. The most decisive are: (1) סוֹדוֹת vs. Ἀποκάλυψις — divine counsels vs. revelation (vv. 1, 20); (2) זְקֵינִים vs. ἐκκλησίαι — elders vs. churches (vv. 4, 11, 20 — three instances); (3) חֶסֶד vs. χάρις — covenant lovingkindness vs. grace (v4); (4) הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן vs. Α καὶ Ω — Isaiah 44:6 quote vs. Greek letter metaphor (vv. 8, 11); (5) נָגִיד וּמְצַוֶּה — the Isaiah 55:4 verbatim quote absent from Greek (v5); (6) כִּדְמוּת אָדָם — Genesis/Ezekiel 'likeness of a man' vs. Daniel/Greek 'son of man' (v13); (7) הַגֵּיהִנֹּם vs. ᾅδου — the Palestinian Valley of Hinnom vs. Greek Hades (v18); (8) שׁוֹרֶה עָלַי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ — Shekinah resting language vs. 'I was in the Spirit' (v10); (9) הַמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת — Zechariah 12:12's 'families' vs. Greek 'tribes' (v7); (10) כֻתּוֹנוֹת — priestly/Genesis 'tunics' vs. descriptive 'foot-length garment' (v13); (11) the חרב פיפיות/מפיו wordplay — sword of mouths from his mouth (v16). The text consistently uses post-biblical Hebrew particles (של, בשביל, עכשיו, אבל, וגם) alongside deeply biblical vocabulary (sodot, chesed, mishkan, nagid, menorot, zekeinim), suggesting an author writing in first-century Hebrew while drawing extensively on the prophetic tradition of Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah. The systematic replacement of zekeinim with ekklesia in the Greek is particularly revealing — the Hebrew author thinks in terms of community leadership (elders), not Greek ecclesial structure (assemblies).
